findings.assertion: The historical government account says construction of the commemorative column was entrusted to Antonio Rivas Mercado in 1900, under a project originally directed by the Secretaría de Comunicaciones y Obras Públicas (SCOP). A 1903 legal transfer placed monuments under Gobernación, so commissioning agency and subsequent oversight must not be conflated.
findings.limitations: Historical government essay; original agency correspondence and 1903 law not checked.

findings.assertion: Rivas Mercado's 1910 inaugural report, as excerpted in the SICT retrospective, specifies two official design constraints: a commemorative column and its siting in the fourth roundabout of Paseo de la Reforma. The siting was a political/urban design decision, not simply an artist's choice.
geographies: Cuarta glorieta, Paseo de la Reforma
findings.source_locator: El Mirador SCOP lines 37–41; identifies García 1911 Crónica Oficial p.74
findings.limitations: Original 1911 printed report and changing numbering of Reforma roundabouts have not been checked against historical maps.

findings.assertion: The first construction attempt suffered differential subsidence in 1906; an INAH register excerpt dates suspension to 12 November 1906 and a renewed cornerstone to 2 April 1909. INBAL's retrospective dates the initial work to January 1902; the SICT text instead says '1892' in its first-stone paragraph. Treat 1892 as an unresolved apparent typographic/transcription discrepancy, not an established cornerstone date.
findings.source_locator: El Mirador lines 15–19,25–31; INBAL 2020 construction excerpt; INAH ficha 12713 indexed 1906/1909 passage
findings.limitations: Original construction ledgers, photographs and official cornerstone invitations not inspected; do not publish exact 1909 refoundation date unqualified.

findings.assertion: Rivas Mercado's reported 1910 material specification identifies grey-blue chiluca from Santo Tomás Tlalmanalco for contrasts of light/shadow. Marble figures were begun in Carrara and finished in Mexico; bronzes were cast in Florence; ornament models were executed in Paris. This is evidence of transatlantic production, not a claim that all visible surviving material is unaltered.
findings.source_locator: El Mirador lines 49–52 and notes 9, citing 1910 Rivas Mercado inaugural report in García 1911
findings.limitations: This is an excerpted architect account, not audited stone provenance or foundry archives; conservation replacements may differ.

findings.assertion: The monument's base has four seated allegories identified as Law, Justice, War and Peace; its lion led by a child was explained by Rivas Mercado as the people strong in war and peaceful in peace. The Victory above bears a laurel and broken chain. These meanings are documented as the designer's stated iconography, not timeless or politically neutral symbols.
geographies: Paseo de la Reforma, Columna de la Independencia
findings.source_locator: El Mirador lines 45–52, attributed to Rivas Mercado 1910 speech, García 1911 pp.74–75
findings.limitations: Check original speech, original 1910 photos and whether all visible sculptures are original vs post-1957 or later restorations.

findings.assertion: After the government inauguration on 16 September 1910, a mechanics-and-railway-workers committee organized a popular procession to the column on 17 September. This complicates a ceremony-only narrative and supplies an example of workers actively appropriating a state monument.
findings.period: Porfirian centenary and labor public space
findings.source_locator: El Mirador lines 55–57, footnote 10 citing Virginia Guedea, Asedio a los Centenarios (2009), p.60
findings.limitations: Original demonstration press coverage, union records and Guedea printed p.60 not directly inspected.

findings.assertion: The column became a mausoleum for independence figures in 1925 according to INBAL's September 2025 release. An INBAL 2020 release contains an internally impossible '1952, under Plutarco Elías Calles' description; that later date must not be recycled as fact. Separate original 1910 monument purpose from 1920s funerary reuse and from later inventory of remains.
findings.source_locator: INBAL bulletin 1105 2025 paragraph on 1925 conversion; INBAL bulletin 2 2020 indexed paragraph on 1952/Calles
findings.limitations: Search-excerpt evidence only; consult 1925 decree and transfer records before editorial corroboration.

findings.assertion: After the 1957 earthquake, engineer Samuel Ruiz installed an interior steel cylinder and central staircase; INBAL says the original quarry-stone courses previously had structural load-bearing functions. Present-day visitor-facing monument fabric therefore includes substantial 20th-century reinforcement and cannot be interpreted wholesale as 1910 construction.
findings.limitations: The structural drawings and original retrofit report have not been inspected; route access/visibility of intervention unverified.

findings.assertion: A September 2017 technical visit after earthquakes found no damage in the marble pavement, bronze/marble sculptures or Victory, but did document internal impacts around the sixth stone course, similar to a third-course issue seen in 2005–06. This does NOT establish present-day 2026 safety or access; it is a dated conservation observation.
findings.limitations: 2017 observational scope only; 2019 and 2024–2025 intervention reports and today's site access not verified.
